text: A chart is an answer to a question. Pick the chart before you know the question, and you'll usually pick the wrong one. This lesson gives you a simple path from question to chart, on a small customer dataset.

Almost every business question fits one of four families. Compare categories, like which segment spends most: use a bar chart. Trend over time, like is revenue growing: use a line chart. Distribution of one variable: use a histogram or box plot. Relationship between two numeric variables: use a scatter plot. A fifth family, part of a whole, is best served by a sorted bar, not a pie with many slices.

On three hundred illustrative retail customers, we answer three questions with three charts from the same data: average spend by segment, the distribution of spend, and the relationship between orders and spend.

The bar chart shows average spend by segment: Basic two hundred forty-one dollars sixty cents, Plus three hundred one forty, Premium four hundred fourteen thirty. Premium customers spend the most, and each step up the ladder is a visible jump.

The histogram shows spend is right-skewed, most customers in the low hundreds with a long tail of bigger spenders. The scatter plot shows more orders going with more spend, the cloud of points sloping clearly upward. Same data, three questions, three natural-fit charts.

For a trend, put time on the x-axis in order and join the points with a line. A line implies order matters and that values in between exist, which is exactly right for time and exactly wrong for unrelated categories like regions.

Common traps: a pie with many slices, a line drawn through categories, two numeric variables shown as separate bar groups instead of a scatter, and picking a chart because it looks impressive. Name the question first. Next: color, layout, and labels, which turn a correct chart into a clear one.
